Keith, a final question for you. You've obviously, you've served in the house. You've been in Congress. If you were going to give some advice to an incoming lawmaker or a staffer who has a prominent role of how to actually view their role in the institution as an important one and when they can make the institution stronger, what advice would you give them? They have to slow things down a little bit so that they can do their job. We live in a culture now that everything is instantaneous, social media, whatever. I think that you have all love and has made this point how members of Congress have basically become mini celebrities. You know, let's get on social media. Let's get on TV. Most of these folks are sitting on TV. I don't know what legislation they've been drafting because frankly, they're not allowed to. That's part of the problem. You've got all these ideas and all this energy bottled up and you don't have an organic process that you're allowing to take place where you could take your idea and actually get it to the floor and have a vote on it. We've had the Hyde Amendment, a provision that restricts taxpayer dollars going to fund abortions for 43 years. Nancy Pelosi did not even allow that amendment to come to the floor. So Republicans had to try to do a motion to recommit to find a way to get it back in. But this is what I've been talking about, where if you're not allowed to even go to the floor and have a debate about something serious and substantive like that, and you're short-circuiting. You're leaving members with no outlet. So they're going to go to social media. They're going to go to the cable shows. And this is where you see this kind of celebrity status set and as opposed to legislating. Again, we need to get back to a set up. Where legislation is actually happening, legislators are empowered to do the job that they're hired to do. So I would encourage anybody who's getting into this right now. Do you want to be a celebrity? Or do you want to legislate? And if you want to legislate, You've got to force your leadership to come up with a way that gives people the ability to do what they think they need to do, whether it's getting on the committee that you think you need to be on. You could take a look at the jurisdiction under a number of these committees and start to break them up. Share the wealth a little bit. There's no reason why all of the committee has to have such a broad subject area. If you have a lot of people who want to be on a committee, well, break it up so that people can get what they ran to Congress to be a part of. I think you'd have better a better legislative product. So yeah, again, I would encourage people to look for ways to actually get legislation done as opposed to simply being the salesperson, the spokesperson for the national party and how it translates to your district. explicit_propositions.text: The founders intended Congress to hold all legislative powers as specified in the Constitution.
Congress has progressively ceded its lawmaking authority to the executive branch over the past century.
Executive branch regulations have the force of law but are not subject to democratic accountability.
The RAINS Act would require Congress to vote on regulations costing $100 million or more.
Leadership frequently bypasses committee processes, delivering legislation directly to the floor.
The current House calendar limits meaningful legislative engagement due to frequent travel and short sessions.
The size of the House has remained fixed at 435 despite a tripling of the U.S. population since 1911.
Increasing the House to 600 members could improve representation and reduce concentration of power.
The non-delegation doctrine is insufficient as a remedy because it relies on judicial interpretation.
Members of Congress are increasingly prioritizing visibility over substantive lawmaking.

assumptions.text: Democratic legitimacy depends on direct citizen accountability for laws, especially costly ones.
Legislative effectiveness requires deliberate, committee-driven processes involving debate and amendments.
A strong Congress is essential to preserving republican self-government and preventing elite technocracy.
Public trust in government declines when decisions are made by unelected officials behind closed doors.
Political leadership values institutional stability over systemic reform, even when reform is needed.
The current system incentivizes partisan spectacle over constructive policymaking.
Reform efforts must involve both Congress and the presidency to succeed.
Representatives are more likely to serve constituents effectively when they spend more time in Washington.
Greater legislative diversity improves policy quality and reduces influence of special interests.
Institutional inertia stems from entrenched power structures benefiting a small coalition of insiders.
